sources.cite: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods, 1.3.5.1 Measures of Location
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 with WebFetch (a summarizing fetch) of the primary page, found by WebSearch. Confirms: extreme values in the tails distort the mean but not the median, which is based on ranks; for data with extreme values in the tails the median is the better estimate of location; in skewed data the mean is pulled toward the tail.

The organization, the systems, the data and the people are fictional. The minutes or days each step takes and the effects of each decision are teaching simplifications for exam practice, not measured values.

brief.situation: You are the analyst at Swiftlane Couriers, a fictional delivery company. The operations director wants this month's delivery performance and a budget recommendation by noon.
handover: Last month: 48,000 deliveries; 120 were held at depots for days during a strike.
North region made 40,000 deliveries; Coastal made 8,000.
howItWorks: The console shows the open dataset, its quality flags and a table of the checks and their results.
Move on a step at a time. A decision comes to you at each step; before the first, you can read the evidence.
At the end you write the record and a short reflection.

then.log: Step 2: customer service finds 120 complaints the report says never happened; the director loses trust in the numbers.
Step 3: extra staff go to North while Coastal's late rate climbs to 13%.
Step 4: overtime doubles; the on-time rate does not move, and the budget is overspent by a quarter of a million dollars.

centerPrompt.title: Mean 2.3 days, median 1.4
centerPrompt.context: A few strike-delayed deliveries pull the mean up.

choices.label: Report the median (1.4 days) with the 90th percentile, show the mean beside it, and explain the 120 strike-delayed deliveries separately

effects.log: The director sees the typical time and the tail.

choices.feedback: Extreme values distort the mean but not the median; for skewed data the median is the better typical value.

choices.label: Report the mean with a footnote about the strike
choices.feedback: Accurate, but the headline overstates the typical delivery.

choices.label: Delete the 120 delayed deliveries and report the new mean
choices.feedback: Real customer experiences vanish from the record.

choices.label: Compare late rates: North 5%, Coastal 10%
choices.feedback: Regions of different sizes are compared by rate, not count.

choices.label: Show counts with the delivery totals beside them
choices.feedback: The information is there, but the reader must do the math.

choices.label: Report North as the worst region by late count
choices.feedback: North is bigger, not worse; Coastal's rate is double.

causePrompt.title: Spend and on-time rate move together
causePrompt.context: Months with more courier overtime spend had better on-time rates (r = 0.7).

choices.label: Report the correlation, note that peak months and new routes also changed, and propose a controlled trial of overtime in two depots
choices.feedback: Correlation does not show cause; other factors moved too, and a test can tell.

choices.label: Report r = 0.7 with no recommendation
choices.feedback: Accurate but leaves the director to guess.

choices.label: Recommend doubling overtime because it causes on-time delivery
choices.feedback: Overtime rose in peak months when routes were also improved; the effect may be the routes.

reflection.question: Write the analysis record for the operations director.

parts.label: Summary statistics
parts.criteria: Median 1.4 days, 90th percentile shown; strike delays explained.
parts.modelAnswer: The typical delivery took 1.4 days (median); 120 strike-delayed deliveries pulled the mean to 2.3 and are reported separately.

parts.label: Comparisons
parts.criteria: Coastal 10% late versus North 5%; correlation, not cause.
parts.modelAnswer: Coastal's late rate is twice North's. Overtime spend correlates with on-time rate, but routes changed too; we propose a two-depot trial.

scoring.modelReasoning: Choose statistics that fit the data: in skewed data the median represents the typical value, and outliers are explained, not deleted. Compare groups of different sizes by rate. Correlation is not causation; propose a test before acting on it.
